title: When someone is unkind
hookLine: a stranger on a late train says she doesn't belong; Arjuna shaking in his chariot; the raised hand on the murtis
carry: your worth isn't up for a vote: abhaya, no fear
last: RAKSHA — A THREAD THAT ASKS FOR PROTECTION.

cards: She was born in this city. She went to school here, works here, loves it. One evening on a late train, a stranger tells her she doesn't really belong here, and throws in a slur meant for a religion that isn't even hers.
Then he gets off at the next stop. She sits there shaking, the train still moving, everyone looking at their phones. A lot of people know a version of that night.
Today, the hard part of a week about neighbors: when one isn't kind.

teach.b: She isn't the first to sit down shaking. The Gita opens with a man doing exactly that.

Arjuna, the great archer, stands in his chariot between two armies, looks across, and falls apart: his limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, his bow slips from his hand, and he sinks down onto the seat.
After one sharp word to stand up, Krishna's answer isn't a plan. It's about who Arjuna is.
The self, he says: weapons can't cut it, fire can't burn it. You met it as the atman on day eight. A stranger's words can shake you.
Much later, Krishna lists the qualities of a godly person, and the very first is abhaya: fearlessness. You can see it on almost any shrine. Ganesha, Durga, Vishnu, one hand raised, palm out.
That's the abhaya mudra. It says: don't be afraid. So here's what the tradition puts in that hand.
Your worth isn't up for a vote.
Dignity, not hate: ahimsa, from day fifteen, is on Krishna's list too, and here it means not answering cruelty with cruelty. It never means staying silent or unsafe. Move away.
Tell someone. Report it. Ask for help.

teach.h: YOU'RE NOT ALONE. US: CALL OR TEXT 988.

teach.b: If you're ever in danger, call local emergency services. If a night like that leaves you somewhere dark, in the US you can call or text 988, any hour, and talk to someone; elsewhere, local emergency help is there too.
This week you visited five houses. The bow from day four still holds, even when someone doesn't bow back.

how: Many murtis of Ganesha, Durga, Vishnu and Shiva show one hand raised, palm out, in the abhaya mudra, the gesture of 'do not fear'.

o: the raised open palm that says: don't be afraid
a palm held up to tell evil to stop
a hand raised to bless a gift being offered

games.q: what's in the raised hand — tap the pairs.
p: sat down shaking, his bow slipping
the self no weapon can cut

s: ahimsa means staying silent when someone is cruel
it means not harming; you can still move away, tell someone and ask for help.
the raised palm on many murtis means do not fear
in the Gita, Krishna puts fearlessness first in his list of godly qualities
abhaya comes first; ahimsa, not harming, is on the list too.

games.q: on a late train, a stranger tells you that you don't belong here. what fits today's teaching?
o: get safe, move away and tell someone; your worth isn't his to decide.
decide he's right and never mention it.
games.why: dignity, not hate: ahimsa means not answering cruelty with cruelty, and it never means staying unsafe or alone.

practice: If you like, lift your right hand, palm out, the way the murtis do, and name a moment someone made you feel small, without reliving it. Breathe in slowly, and on the out-breath let the hand say what it says: don't be afraid.
If you pray, you can ask for courage; if you don't, let the steady breath be the answer. Lower your hand when you're ready.

wordCard.voice: Abhaya mudra. The raised open palm on so many murtis: no fear, don't be afraid. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: abhaya, no fear, and mudra, a gesture. the raised palm on many murtis.

carryVoice: Your line: your worth isn't up for a vote. Abhaya, no fear. Nobody on a train gets to decide it. See you tomorrow.
